content: The progression of β-cell destruction in immune-mediated diabetes can vary greatly among individuals. In certain cases, particularly in children, the destruction of β-cells occurs at a rapid pace. This often results in the early onset of severe hyperglycemia and the development of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In contrast, adults with immune-mediated diabetes may retain partial β-cell function for a longer duration. This residual β-cell activity can initially prevent the occurrence of DKA. However, as the disease progresses and β-cell function continues to decline, these individuals eventually become insulin-dependent and face an increased risk of developing DKA. In the later stages of type 1 diabetes, plasma C-peptide levels are typically low or undetectable. This finding reflects minimal or absent endogenous insulin production, which is a hallmark of advanced β-cell destruction.
